question: My maize is at knee height and the young leaves have ragged holes with wet sawdust-like droppings in the funnel. About a third of the plants look affected. I farm one acre in central Uganda and the rains started three weeks ago. What is attacking my crop?
answer: Those signs point strongly to fall armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda). Larvae hide in the leaf whorl (funnel) and leave moist frass that looks like wet sawdust, plus irregular holes on young leaves. Confirm by gently opening a few whorls at dusk or early morning and looking for green-brown caterpillars with a dark head and a pale inverted Y on the face. Act this week: (1) hand-pick and crush larvae in heavily hit plants if labour is available; (2) apply a recommended insecticide labelled for FAW in maize at the correct rate, targeting the whorl—early morning or late afternoon; (3) if you can afford only one intervention, prioritise a single well-timed whorl-directed spray on the worst third of the field before larvae grow large. Avoid spraying randomly across dry leaves only. Scout again after 3–5 days. Rotate products next spray to reduce resistance. Contact your local extension officer for products currently recommended in your district.

question: I harvested 900 kg of beans and want to store them until prices rise in three months, but last season I lost a lot to weevils and some bags went mouldy. I have no electricity and store in a mud-brick room. How should I dry and store them?
answer: Dry thoroughly first, then protect from insects and moisture. (1) Spread beans in a thin layer on clean tarpaulins or raised racks in sun for several days; stir often. They are dry enough when you cannot easily dent a seed with a thumbnail, and a sample of 20–30 beans feels hard and sounds glassy when bitten or shaken—aim for about 12–14% moisture without a meter. (2) Winnow and remove broken, mouldy, or insect-damaged grains. (3) Use clean, dry Purdue Improved Crop Storage (PICS) or other hermetic bags if available; fill, press out air, and seal tightly. If only ordinary bags, use new jute/poly bags lined with polythene, and consider an approved grain protectant or diatomaceous earth mixed as recommended. (4) Stack bags on pallets or poles off the mud floor, away from walls, under a leak-free roof. (5) Check monthly for heating, musty smell, or live weevils; if found, re-dry and re-bag. Never store damp beans—mould and aflatoxin risk rises fast in humid rooms.

question: My cassava leaves are yellow-mottled and curled, and plants are stunted. Neighbours say it is mosaic. Can I still harvest roots, and what should I plant next season?
answer: Yellow mottling, leaf distortion, and stunting are classic cassava mosaic disease (CMD) symptoms, usually spread by whiteflies and infected cuttings. Roots from mildly affected plants may still be usable if firm and not rotten, but yields will be lower; discard severely stunted plants. Do not take cuttings from diseased plants. Next season: (1) source CMD-resistant or tolerant varieties released for your zone from a trusted nursery or research station; (2) plant only healthy, uniform cuttings; (3) remove and destroy volunteer diseased plants early; (4) avoid overlapping old infected fields with new plantings when possible. Ask NAADS/extension which resistant varieties perform well in your district.

question: On my arabica coffee in Nyeri, green berries are getting dark sunken spots and some are rotting on the tree. What is this and what can I do before the next rains?
answer: Dark sunken lesions on green berries that progress to rot often indicate coffee berry disease (Colletotrichum kahawae), especially in cool, wet highland areas like Nyeri. Confirm with an agronomist if unsure (other berry pests exist). Before rains intensify: (1) strip and destroy highly infected berries if labour allows; (2) improve air flow by pruning and managing shade; (3) apply a recommended copper or other labelled fungicide on the schedule advised for CBD in your area, covering berries thoroughly; (4) ensure good drainage and avoid excessive nitrogen that keeps soft tissue vulnerable. Keep records of sprays and harvest separately from heavily diseased trees if quality is affected.

question: Some banana plants yellow from the bottom leaves up, then the stem splits and a foul smell comes when I cut it. Is this banana wilt, and how do I stop it spreading?
answer: Bottom-up yellowing, stem splitting, and foul-smelling internal rot are consistent with banana bacterial wilt (Xanthomonas wilt) common in Uganda. Stop spread immediately: (1) do not cut or move tools between plants without sterilising (flame or disinfectant); (2) remove male buds early with a forked stick, not a shared knife if possible; (3) uproot and destroy infected mats as advised by extension—do not feed fresh infected material carelessly to animals in ways that move disease; (4) avoid sharing suckers from infected fields; (5) plant healthy tissue-culture or certified suckers into clean land. Report outbreaks to local agricultural officers for district guidance.

question: I plant maize on 2 acres in western Kenya. When should I apply DAP and CAN, and how much if I have a limited budget?
answer: With a limited budget, prioritise basal phosphorus at planting and a single well-timed nitrogen top-dress. Typical smallholder pattern (adjust to soil test and county advice): (1) at planting, place DAP (or NPK with P) in the planting hole or furrow beside the seed—not touching the seed—at a reduced rate if cash is short rather than skipping P entirely on depleted soils; (2) top-dress CAN or urea when maize is about knee-high / 3–5 weeks after emergence, when rains are reliable. Split nitrogen only if you can afford two applications. Never broadcast urea on dry soil with no rain expected. Combine with manure if available. Ask your county extension for exact kg/acre for your variety and rainfall.

question: When should I plant maize in Morogoro for the main rains, and how deep should I plant the seed?
answer: Plant at the reliable onset of the main rains for your ward—often after soils are moist to planting depth for several days, not after a single light shower. Exact calendar weeks vary year to year; follow local seasonal forecasts and extension alerts. Plant seed about 3–5 cm deep in moist soil (deeper in very light sandy soils if the surface dries fast; shallower in heavy wet clay). Use recommended spacing for your variety (commonly around 75 cm between rows and 25–30 cm within row for many hybrids—confirm on the seed pack). Avoid planting into waterlogged fields.

question: Bean seedlings are wilting in patches after heavy rain. Roots look brown and rotten. What can I do this season and next?
answer: Patchy wilt after waterlogging with brown roots suggests root rot complexes (often Fusarium/Pythium/Rhizoctonia), worse in poorly drained soils and continuous bean cropping. This season: improve surface drainage, avoid further irrigation/flooding, and remove badly wilted plants. Do not expect a curative spray to revive rotten roots. Next season: rotate away from beans for a cycle if possible; plant on ridges or raised beds; use certified seed of more tolerant varieties if available; avoid planting too deep in cold wet soil; incorporate well-rotted compost rather than fresh residues that stay wet.

question: How long should cassava cuttings be, and how do I plant them for better establishment?
answer: Use mature, healthy stems (pencil-thick or thicker) from disease-free plants. Cuttings are commonly 20–30 cm with several nodes. Plant at the start of reliable rains into moist soil. Orientation: place cuttings at a slant or vertically with several nodes buried so buds can sprout; follow local extension preference for your soil. Space according to variety (often about 1 m × 1 m for many systems). Do not use cuttings from mosaic- or brown-streak-symptomatic plants. Weed early until canopy covers.

question: My coffee bushes are tall and crowded. When and how should I prune for better yield?
answer: Prune to keep a manageable canopy, improve light and air (reduces disease), and renew productive wood. After main harvest, remove dead, diseased, and crossing branches; thin crowded suckers; keep the height you can spray and pick comfortably. For multi-stem systems, retain a few strong stems and cycle older ones over years as advised for robusta or arabica in your area. Always use sharp clean tools; sterilise between trees if wilt or other systemic disease is present in the garden. Combine pruning with shade management—neither dense shade nor harsh full sun extremes.

question: Purple witchweed is flowering in my maize field and plants look yellow and weak. What helps against striga?
answer: Striga (witchweed) attaches to maize roots and steals nutrients, causing yellowing and poor ears. Integrated control: (1) hand-pull flowering striga before it sheds seed—bag and burn or bury deeply; (2) rotate with non-host crops (e.g. some legumes/cereals as locally recommended) and use catch/trap crops where advised; (3) improve soil fertility with manure and appropriate fertiliser—striga hits harder on poor soils; (4) plant striga-tolerant maize varieties if released for your county; (5) consider herbicide seed dressings or IR-maize systems only where officially promoted and you can follow the protocol. One season of pulling alone will not empty the seedbank—persist for several seasons.

question: Banana leaves are yellowing but it does not look like wilt. Could it be lack of nutrients?
answer: Uniform yellowing, especially older leaves, with no foul stem rot can indicate nitrogen deficiency or general poor fertility; striped or patchy patterns may point to other nutrients or pests. Check for weevils, nematodes, and waterlogging too. Practical response: apply well-rotted manure or compost around the mat (not piled against the pseudostem), mulch to keep moisture, and follow local fertiliser recommendations for banana if you can afford mineral NPK. Ensure mats are not overcrowded—de-sucker to recommended plants per mat. If unsure between nutrient deficiency and Xanthomonas wilt, cut a suspect stem carefully with a sterilised tool and look for yellow bacterial ooze and foul smell.

question: Black sunken spots on bean pods and stems appeared after cool wet weather. Is it anthracnose?
answer: Sunken black/brown lesions on pods, stems, and sometimes leaves in cool wet conditions often indicate anthracnose (Colletotrichum). Use certified disease-free seed next season; avoid saving seed from badly spotted pods. This season: remove heavily infected debris after harvest; avoid working the crop when wet; consider a labelled fungicide if disease is early and weather stays wet—follow extension guidance. Rotate fields and choose more resistant varieties when available.

question: How do I reduce aflatoxin risk in maize after harvest without a dryer?
answer: Aflatoxin fungi grow when grain is damp and warm. (1) Harvest on time—do not leave cobs drying forever in the field if rains return. (2) Dry quickly to safe moisture (maize typically ~13% or below): sun-dry on tarpaulins, raise off soil, stir often, protect from night dew. (3) Sort out mouldy, discoloured, and insect-damaged grains before storage. (4) Store in clean dry hermetic bags or well-ventilated dry cribs off the floor. (5) Never mix wet new grain into dry old stores. Discard heavily mouldy grain rather than feeding or selling it—aflatoxin is not removed by ordinary cooking.

question: Cassava roots have yellow-brown dry rotten patches inside even when leaves look almost normal. What is that?
answer: Dry yellow-brown necrotic patches in roots with relatively mild leaf signs can indicate cassava brown streak disease (CBSD), a serious virus problem in parts of East Africa. Confirm with extension. Do not use stems from affected plants as cuttings. Plant CBSD-tolerant varieties where recommended; source clean planting material; remove infected plants early when identified. Roots with extensive necrosis should not be used for food or sale.

question: Orange powdery spots on the underside of coffee leaves—is that leaf rust?
answer: Orange-yellow powdery pustules mainly on the underside of leaves are typical of coffee leaf rust (Hemileia vastatrix). It defoliates trees and cuts yield. Manage with resistant varieties where available, balanced nutrition, sensible shade, and timely fungicide programmes recommended for your altitude and rainfall. Collect and destroy heavily infected fallen leaves if practical. Monitor after rainy periods.

question: If I plant maize too densely, what goes wrong, and what spacing is safer for a drought-prone area?
answer: Overly dense maize competes for water and nitrogen, stays leafy, and produces small ears—especially risky in drought-prone zones. Prefer the spacing on your seed label; if drought risk is high, lean toward slightly wider within-row spacing rather than crowding. Ensure one healthy plant per station after thinning. Pair sensible population with early weed control and fertiliser you can afford.

question: Should I plant beans at the very start of rains or wait a bit in central Uganda?
answer: Plant into moist soil at a reliable onset of rains so germination is even, but avoid sowing into waterlogged sticky clay after extreme downpours. For many areas, planting early in the season helps escape late pests and terminal drought—but follow local calendar advice for your parish. Use certified seed and inoculant if recommended for your soil. Weed early (first 2–3 weeks are critical).

question: Banana stems have tunnels and plants tip over easily. Could it be banana weevil?
answer: Tunnels in the corm/pseudostem base and lodging often indicate banana weevil. Sanitation is key: pare suckers before planting, remove old harvested pseudostems, trap adults with split pseudostem traps, and keep fields clean. Use clean planting material. Some insecticides are used as directed by extension for severe infestations—follow label and local rules. Combine with nematode management and good nutrition for stronger mats.

question: Rectangular grey lesions on maize leaves spreading up the plant in humid weather—what is it?
answer: Rectangular grey to tan lesions running between veins in humid conditions often indicate grey leaf spot (Cercospora). Yield loss rises if lesions reach upper leaves before grain fill. Use resistant hybrids when possible; rotate crops; bury or remove residue where practical; apply fungicide only if extension confirms economic risk and weather stays favourable for disease. Avoid excessive late nitrogen that keeps canopies wet and dense.

question: Can I intercrop cassava with beans, and what spacing helps both?
answer: Yes—cassava–bean intercrops are common. Plant cassava at its normal wide spacing and sow beans in the alleys early so beans mature before cassava shades them heavily. Do not overcrowd; both crops need light and nutrients. Weed carefully. Use disease-free cassava cuttings and clean bean seed. Ask local extension for arrangements that fit your variety maturity.

question: Coffee leaves are pale and yields dropped. I apply little fertiliser. What is a practical nutrition plan?
answer: Coffee responds to organic matter plus mineral nutrients matched to yield removal. Practical steps: maintain mulch; apply available manure/compost annually around the drip line; follow district fertiliser rates for NPK if you can buy inputs—split nitrogen applications rather than one heavy dose. Correct pH issues with lime only if soil tests or extension recommend it. Nutrient deficiency alone can mimic disease—rule out leaf rust and pests too.

question: Bean shoots are curled and covered with small soft insects. What should I do?
answer: Those are likely aphids. They suck sap and can spread viruses. For light infestations, a strong water spray or insecticidal soap/plant extracts used safely can help; encourage natural enemies by avoiding unnecessary broad sprays. For heavy infestations on young crops, use a recommended aphicide per label. Remove heavily infested shoot tips if practical. Plant certified seed and control weeds that host aphids.

question: How is maize stalk borer different from fall armyworm, and what do I look for?
answer: Fall armyworm usually feeds in the whorl of younger plants with frass in the funnel and ragged leaves. Stalk borers (e.g. Busseola/Chilo) bore into stems, causing deadhearts, tunnels, and lodging later. Look for entry holes, frass on stems, and broken plants. Control includes resistant varieties, timely planting, destroying infected stubble, and targeted insecticides when thresholds are met—follow local IPM guidance. Correct identification matters so you treat the right pest stage.

question: How far apart should I plant banana mats on a small hillside plot?
answer: Common spacings are about 3 m × 3 m for many cooking banana systems, adjusted for variety and fertility—closer spacing needs more manure and water. On hillsides, plant on contours, maintain mulch to stop erosion, and dig basins that catch water without waterlogging the corm. Keep recommended suckers per mat. Ask local extension for variety-specific spacing.

question: Is recycled hybrid maize seed from last harvest okay to plant?
answer: Recycled hybrid grain is not recommended. Hybrid vigour and uniformity drop in F2, so yields and stress tolerance usually fall. Buy certified hybrid seed each season when possible. If cost forces farm-saved seed, understand you are accepting lower performance; at least select from healthy disease-free ears, dry well, and treat seed if advised. Prefer OPVs only if they are true open-pollinated varieties meant for saving.

question: How do I know when cassava is ready to harvest for home food?
answer: Maturity depends on variety—many are ready from about 8–12 months, some longer. Check a few plants by carefully digging: roots should have developed usable size with good starch for your variety. Harvest for home use as needed rather than leaving roots too long if brown streak or rotting risk is high in your area. Process soon after harvest for fresh products; dry chips properly if storing.

question: Should I pick all coffee cherries at once or selectively?
answer: For quality arabica, selective picking of ripe red cherries is preferred—under-ripe and over-ripe fruit hurt cup quality and price at many factories. Pick in rounds as cherries ripen. Keep cherry clean, deliver quickly, and avoid mixing with soil or leaves. Follow your cooperative’s receiving rules.

question: Do beans need fertiliser if I already grow them with rhizobia nodules?
answer: Beans can fix nitrogen if well nodulated, but they still often respond to phosphorus at planting on deficient soils, and to starter nutrients. Check nodules: healthy ones are pink inside. On poor soils, a small basal P application and manure help more than heavy nitrogen, which can reduce fixation. Follow soil-test or extension rates for your parish.

question: When is the most important time to weed maize?
answer: The most critical window is the first 3–6 weeks after emergence, before weeds outcompete seedlings for water and nutrients. Weed early and thoroughly; a second weeding before canopy closure helps. Late weeding after maize is tall recovers less yield. Mulch or cover crops can reduce later weed pressure where systems allow.

question: Is mulching banana worth it in a dry season, and what should I use?
answer: Yes. Mulch conserves moisture, feeds soil, and reduces erosion. Use dry grass, crop residues, or banana trash arranged around the mat but not piled tightly against the pseudostem base (reduces rot and weevil shelter). Replenish as it decomposes. Combine with manure for better response.

question: How much shade should robusta coffee have?
answer: Moderate shade often helps robusta against heat and some stress, but heavy shade reduces yield and can worsen fungal disease by keeping leaves wet. Aim for dappled light—manage shade trees by pruning. Exact levels depend on altitude and rainfall; follow local coffee officer advice for your district.

question: Rains failed mid-season and maize is rolling leaves at tasseling. What can I still do?
answer: Leaf rolling is a water-stress response. If soils may still receive late rain, reduce further competition: weed, and avoid heavy late nitrogen that the crop cannot use. There is no spray that replaces water. For salvage, some fields still produce small ears—prioritise household food. Next season: choose earlier-maturing varieties, plant on time, consider moisture-conserving practices (zai pits, mulch, reduced tillage where suitable), and lower plant population slightly.

question: Cassava leaves are webbed and skeletonised by small caterpillars. What pest is that?
answer: Webbing and skeletonised leaves often indicate cassava green mite or, with webbing/caterpillars, cassava mealybug or lepidopteran defoliators depending on exact signs—inspect closely. For mites, avoid unnecessary broad insecticides that kill predators; maintain field hygiene and use tolerant varieties. For severe outbreaks, follow IPM recommendations from NARO/extension. Correct ID matters before spraying.

question: When should I harvest climbing beans to reduce shattering losses?
answer: Harvest when most pods are dry and yellow-brown but before pods shatter in the sun. Pick in rounds if maturity is uneven. Dry pods further on tarpaulins if needed, then thresh gently. Store only dry clean grain. Avoid leaving mature pods through heavy late rains.

question: I store maize on the cob in a raised crib. How do I keep it safer from mould and rodents?
answer: Ensure the crib is raised, well ventilated, and rainproof. Load only well-dried cobs; remove husks if that is your system’s practice for faster drying—follow local proven methods. Keep surroundings clean, trim vegetation, and use rodent guards on posts. Do not add wet cobs on top of dry ones. Check for heating and mouldy smells; remove bad cobs promptly.

question: When does stumping old coffee make sense?
answer: Stumping (cutting back old stems to renew growth) helps exhausted, unproductive trees if roots are healthy and you can manage the yield gap while new stems grow. Do it after harvest, in sections of the farm so income continues. Follow cooperative/extension protocols for height, fertiliser after stumping, and disease control on new shoots. Do not stump trees dying from wilt without diagnosis.

question: How do I tell when a cooking banana bunch is ready?
answer: Fingers become rounded and full for the variety, ridges less sharp, and colour/maturity marks match local market preference. Harvest with a clean cut, support the bunch, and handle gently to avoid bruising. Do not leave over-mature bunches that split or attract pests. Transport promptly.

question: Maize lower leaves are yellow in a V-shape from the tip. Is that nitrogen deficiency?
answer: Yellowing of older leaves starting at the tip and forming a V along the midrib is a classic nitrogen deficiency pattern. Confirm by checking overall pale colour and poor growth. Respond with a timely top-dress of CAN/urea when moisture is available, plus organic matter for longer-term fertility. Rule out striga and waterlogging, which can look similar.

question: What is rhizobium inoculant and should I use it on beans?
answer: Rhizobium inoculant coats seed with bacteria that form nodules and fix nitrogen. It helps most on soils where the right rhizobia are few—often new fields or where beans have not been grown. Keep inoculant cool, apply in shade, plant soon after treatment, and avoid mixing with harsh chemicals on seed unless the product allows it. Still supply phosphorus if soils are deficient.

question: How should I dry cassava chips so they store without mould?
answer: Peel, wash, and chip healthy roots; sun-dry on clean raised surfaces until chips snap cleanly and feel dry through the centre. Protect from dew and rain; stir for even drying. Store in clean dry bags off the floor. Discard roots with brown streak necrosis. Poor drying causes mould and losses.

question: My coffee is on a slope and soil washes every rain. What low-cost steps help?
answer: Establish contour grass strips or terraces as locally promoted; keep mulch under coffee; avoid bare clean weeding that leaves soil exposed; plant cover or shade thoughtfully; dig runoff diversion above the garden if safe. Erosion removes fertiliser you paid for—mulch and ground cover are high-return practices.

question: Besides spraying, what cultural methods reduce fall armyworm next season?
answer: Plant with the main rains so plants are not the only green host; keep fields weed-free early; encourage natural enemies by avoiding calendar spraying; rotate crops; destroy heavily infested residues if advised; scout twice weekly in the vegetative stage. Use pheromone traps for monitoring where available. Insecticide is a last or targeted tool, not the only tool.

question: How many suckers should I leave on a banana mat?
answer: Many cooking banana systems keep about 3 plants per mat (mother, daughter, granddaughter) and remove extras. Exact recommendations vary by variety and fertility—overcrowding reduces bunch size. De-sucker regularly with clean tools. On wilt-affected farms, minimise knife use between mats; prefer breaking suckers by hand methods taught by extension.

question: How do PICS bags work for bean storage?
answer: PICS and similar hermetic bags have layered liners that limit oxygen so insects cannot thrive—without always needing chemical protectants. Fill with clean dry beans, press out air, seal each liner tightly, then close the outer bag. Store off the floor in a dry place. Do not puncture liners. If beans were not dry enough, mould can still grow—dryness first.

question: I cannot afford a full lab soil test every year. What should I do instead?
answer: Prioritise a test when starting a new plot or after years of poor response to fertiliser. Between tests: add manure/compost, follow county fertiliser blends as a baseline, watch crop deficiency symptoms, and keep simple records of rates and yields. Avoid dumping only nitrogen every year on acidic or P-deficient soils. Ask cooperatives about subsidised testing campaigns.

question: Cassava grows slowly at first. How important is early weeding?
answer: Critical. Young cassava does not shade weeds well. Weed within the first months until canopy covers. Later weeds still steal water but early competition hurts establishment most. Mulch can help where residues are available. Avoid damaging cuttings when hoeing.

question: What does IPM mean for a small coffee farmer in practice?
answer: Integrated Pest Management means monitoring first, then combining cultural practices (pruning, sanitation, shade), resistant varieties, biological allies, and chemicals only when thresholds justify cost. For coffee: strip diseased berries, prune for air flow, scout for pests, and spray fungicides/insecticides on a need basis with correct nozzles and PPE. Calendar spraying without scouting wastes money and can worsen outbreaks.

question: What should I rotate with maize on one acre to improve soil and break pests?
answer: Rotate maize with legumes (beans, soyabean, groundnuts) where markets and rainfall allow—legumes can add nitrogen and break some pest/disease cycles. Avoid maize-after-maize forever on the same beds. Include a deep-rooted or different family crop when possible. Match rotation to food security needs; even a partial field rotation helps.

question: I got conflicting advice from a neighbour and an agro-dealer about a pesticide. What should I trust?
answer: Prefer labelled products registered for your crop and pest, at the rate and pre-harvest interval on the label. Cross-check with a government extension officer or cooperative agronomist. Neighbour experience is useful for local timing, but wrong products or doses cause resistance, residues, and crop damage. Keep the label; wear PPE; never reuse chemical containers for food or water.

question: Mahindi yangu yana mashimo kwenye majani na kinyesi kwenye kituo cha jani. Ni nini na nifanye nini?
answer: Dalili hizo mara nyingi ni kiwavi wa fall armyworm anayekaa ndani ya kituo cha jani (whorl). Hakikisha kwa kufungua majani asubuhi. Chukua hatua haraka: ondoka viwavi kwa mkono kama unaweza; nyunyiza dawa iliyopendekezwa kwa FAW kwenye kituo cha jani asubuhi au jioni; fuatilia baada ya siku 3–5. Usinyunyize ovyo bila kupima. Consiliana na afisa ugani wa kata kwa dawa zinazoruhusiwa.

question: Nilivuna maharagwe na ninataka kuyahifadhi miezi mitatu bila umeme. Nifanye nini?
answer: Kausha vizuri kwanza hadi maharagwe yawe magumu (haziwezi kubanwa kirahisi). pepeta, ondoa yaliyooza au yaliyoharibiwa. Tumia mifuko ya hermetic (kama PICS) ikiwa inapatikana—funga kwa nguvu baada ya kutoa hewa. Weka mifuko juu ya mbao, mbali na unyevu wa sakafu. Kagua kila mwezi kwa wadudu na ukungu. Usuhifadhi maharagwe yaliyo na unyevu.

question: How much manure should I put on each banana mat per year if that is all I can afford?
answer: Rates vary, but many smallholder recommendations are on the order of one to several basins/debe of well-rotted manure per mat per year, applied in a ring under the mulch—not fresh hot manure against the stem. Consistency beats one huge dump. Combine with de-suckering and mulching. If manure is scarce, prioritise weaker mats and newly planted holes.

question: I want to raise coffee seedlings. What basics matter for a small nursery?
answer: Use certified seed or seedlings from trusted sources; fill pots with well-drained mix; provide light shade; water evenly without waterlogging; harden seedlings before field planting; rogue diseased or off-type plants. Plant in the field at the onset of reliable rains with good hole preparation and mulch. Avoid mystery seedlings of unknown variety.

question: Is it safe to use herbicide on maize when I also intercrop beans?
answer: Many maize herbicides injure beans. Only use products labelled for your exact intercrop system, or weed mechanically/with a hoe in intercrops. If spraying sole maize, shield non-target crops and follow wind and timing rules. When unsure, ask extension before buying—wrong herbicide can kill the bean crop.

question: What simple records should a smallholder keep to improve next season?
answer: Write planting dates, variety/seed source, fertiliser and chemical rates with dates, rainfall notes, pest outbreaks, and yields per plot. Even a notebook helps you see what paid off. Keep purchase receipts for inputs. Share summaries with your farmer group or extension agent when seeking advice.

question: Fresh cassava roots do not keep long. How should I plan harvest for market?
answer: Harvest to match known buyers or processing days—fresh roots deteriorate in a few days. For longer holding, process into dried chips or flour after proper drying. Agree volumes with buyers beforehand when possible. Sort out diseased or fibrous roots. Transport in clean containers; avoid bruising.

question: Should I grow climbing or bush beans on a small plot with stakes available?
answer: Climbing beans often yield more per area if you can stake and manage labour; bush beans need less staking and mature faster for quick food/cash. Choose based on labour, stake supply, and market. Use certified seed of varieties released for your altitude. Stake early so vines climb cleanly.

question: Where do most maize losses happen after harvest on small farms, and how do I cut them?
answer: Big losses come from delayed drying, mould, insects in store, rodents, and spillage. Cut them by harvesting on time, drying to safe moisture, sorting, using hermetic or well-managed stores, elevating bags, and controlling rodents. Measure what you put in store versus what you take out so you see the real loss.

question: Rains feel more unreliable. What practical farm adjustments help without expensive tech?
answer: Diversify crops and varieties (including earlier-maturing ones); stagger planting on part of the land; use mulch and organic matter to hold moisture; repair soil cover on slopes; keep small livestock or kitchen gardens as buffers; follow local seasonal forecasts from meteorological/extension services; avoid investing all fertiliser on a late risky planting. Record what worked in dry years.
